claim: Tk-GAL4FruM neurons are male-specific fru-expressing neurons that promote male-type aggressive behavior upon activation.
source: Tk-GAL4FruM neurons are fru-expressing, male-specific neurons that are not only capable of promoting male-type aggressive behavior, but also are necessary for spontaneous male aggression (Asahina et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Asahina et al., 2014, which provides published evidence for the claim.

claim: Tk-GAL4FruM neurons are necessary for spontaneous male aggression.
source: Tk-GAL4FruM neurons are fru-expressing, male-specific neurons that are not only capable of promoting male-type aggressive behavior, but also are necessary for spontaneous male aggression (Asahina et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Asahina et al., 2014.

claim: Optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in males induces robust aggression toward male target flies during LED stimulation.
source: The tester flies in which CsChrimson was expressed under the control of Tk-GAL41 within the brain (which phenocopies the manipulation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons; Asahina et al., 2014) showed robust aggression toward the target male flies, mainly during LED stimulation (Figure 1 C2, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A2; Watanabe et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 C2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A2, as well as citations to Asahina et al., 2014 and Watanabe et al., 2017.

claim: Optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons increases time orienting toward male target flies.
source: This coincides with increased time orienting toward the target fly (Figure 1C1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A1), but wing extension toward males was not affected (Figure 1C3, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A3; see also Video 1 – Part 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A1.

claim: Optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons does not affect wing extension toward male targets.
source: This coincides with increased time orienting toward the target fly (Figure 1C1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A1), but wing extension toward males was not affected (Figure 1C3, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A3; see also Video 1 – Part 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C3 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A3.

claim: Optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons does not induce lunges toward female target flies.
source: In contrast, we observed no lunges toward female target flies after the same optogenetic manipulations (Figure 1D2, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B2.

claim: Optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons increases time orienting toward female target flies during LED stimulation.
source: The tester flies increased the time orienting toward the target female during LED stimulations (Figure 1D1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B1; see also Video 1 – Part 2), suggesting that the activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons can promote interaction regardless of the sex of the target fly.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B1.

claim: Activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons can promote interaction regardless of the sex of the target fly.
source: The tester flies increased the time orienting toward the target female during LED stimulations (Figure 1D1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B1; see also Video 1 – Part 2), suggesting that the activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons can promote interaction regardless of the sex of the target fly.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that orienting time increases toward both male and female targets.

claim: Optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons does not induce lunges in the absence of a target fly.
source: Neither did we observe lunges when Tk-GAL41-labeled neurons were optogenetically activated in the absence of any target fly (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons induces lunges strictly when a male target fly is present.
source: Thus, the activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons induces lunges strictly when a male target fly is present.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observations that lunges occur with male targets but not with female targets or in the absence of targets.

claim: Tester flies performed less wing extensions toward target females during LED stimulation than during inter-stimulus intervals.
source: In addition, we observed that tester flies performed less wing extensions toward target females during LED stimulation than during ISIs (Figure 1D3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D3.

claim: The total amount of wing extensions toward female targets was not significantly different from genetic controls.
source: However, the total amount of wing extensions was not significantly different from those of the two genetic controls.
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of experimental and control groups.

claim: Tk-GAL4FruM neurons are specified only in males.
source: As was previously shown (Asahina et al., 2014), Tk-GAL4FruM neurons are specified only in males (Figure 1G,J).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Asahina et al., 2014 and data shown in Figure 1G,J.

claim: fruM females show lunges and other male-type aggressive actions.
source: fruM females are reported to show lunges and other male-type aggressive actions (Vrontou et al., 2006), suggesting that fru is the chief architect of neural circuits underlying sexually dimorphism in aggressive behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Vrontou et al., 2006.

claim: fru is the chief architect of neural circuits underlying sexual dimorphism in aggressive behavior.
source: fruM females are reported to show lunges and other male-type aggressive actions (Vrontou et al., 2006), suggesting that fru is the chief architect of neural circuits underlying sexually dimorphism in aggressive behavior.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that fruM females show male-type aggression and citation to Vrontou et al., 2006.

claim: Male-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons are not specified in fruM females.
source: However, two fru-expressing, aggression-promoting neurons (male-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons (Koganezawa et al., 2016) and P1a neurons Hoopfer et al., 2015) are not specified in this genotype (see Ishii et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Koganezawa et al., 2016, Hoopfer et al., 2015, and Ishii et al., 2020.

claim: P1a neurons are not specified in fruM females.
source: However, two fru-expressing, aggression-promoting neurons (male-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons (Koganezawa et al., 2016) and P1a neurons Hoopfer et al., 2015) are not specified in this genotype (see Ishii et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hoopfer et al., 2015 and Ishii et al., 2020.

claim: Not all fru-expressing neurons underlie the sexual dimorphism of aggressive actions.
source: These observations strongly suggest that not all fru-expressing neurons underlie the sexual dimorphism of aggressive actions, even if the activation of such neurons in a normal male induces male-type aggressive behavior.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that some fru-expressing neurons are not specified in fruM females despite these flies showing male-type aggression.

claim: Tk-GAL4FruM neurons were present in fruM females.
source: In contrast to male-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons or P1a neurons, Tk-GAL4FruM neurons were present in fruM females (Figure 1H), but not in fruF males (Figure 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Tk-GAL4FruM neurons were not present in fruF males.
source: In contrast to male-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons or P1a neurons, Tk-GAL4FruM neurons were present in fruM females (Figure 1H), but not in fruF males (Figure 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: FruM protein is expressed in Tk-GAL4FruM neurons.
source: Consistent with this observation, we detected expression of FruM, but not Dsx, proteins in Tk-GAL4FruM neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: Dsx protein is not expressed in Tk-GAL4FruM neurons.
source: Consistent with this observation, we detected expression of FruM, but not Dsx, proteins in Tk-GAL4FruM neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: The cell body number of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in fruM females was indistinguishable from that in males.
source: The cell body number of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in fruM females was indistinguishable from that in males (Figure 1K).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: The averaged morphology of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons from males and fruM females appeared virtually identical.
source: The averaged morphology of registered Tk-GAL4FruM neurons from males (Figure 1L) and from fruM females (Figure 1M) appeared virtually identical (Video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by registered and averaged imaging data shown in Figure 1L, 1M, and Video 3.

claim: None of the three prominent neurite processes of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons showed significant difference in volume among fru +/+ control males, fruM/fru4-40 males, and fruM females.
source: None of these three processes showed significant difference in volume among fru +/+ control males, fruM/fru4-40 males, and fruM females (Figure 1N–P).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative volume measurements shown in Figure 1N–P.

claim: Tk-GAL4FruM neurons are specified predominantly by fru.
source: While we acknowledge that this approach might miss finer scale differences in neuroanatomy, we conclude that Tk-GAL4FruM neurons are specified predominantly by fru.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the anatomical and cell count data showing that Tk-GAL4FruM neurons are present and morphologically similar in fruM females and males.

claim: dsx and fru have clearly separable roles for the specification of neuronal populations that are important for Drosophila aggressive behaviors.
source: dsx and fru therefore have clearly separable roles for the specification of neuronal populations that are important for Drosophila aggressive behaviors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential effects of dsx and fru on specification of different aggression-related neuronal populations.

claim: Presence of the fru4-40 allele did not affect cell number or overall morphology of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons.
source: Presence of the fru4-40 allele did not affect cell number or overall morphology of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons (Figure 1K, Figure 1—figure supplement 2F–M).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 1K and Figure 1—figure supplement 2F–M.

claim: Activation of Tk-GAL41-labeled neurons triggered similar behavioral changes in the backgrounds of +/+, +/fru4-40, or fruM/fru4-40 males.
source: Consistent with this, the activation of Tk-GAL41-labeled neurons triggered similar behavioral changes in the backgrounds of +/+, +/fru4-40, or fruM/fru4-40 males (Figure 1—figure supplement 2N).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2N.

claim: Heterozygosity of fruM resulted in incomplete specification of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in a chromosomally female background.
source: However, heterozygosity of fruM resulted in incomplete specification of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in a chromosomally female background (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C.

claim: fruFLP is a hypomorphic allele.
source: We also found that fruFLP, a knock-in allele of fru that expresses a DNA recombinase Flippase (Yu et al., 2010), is hypomorphic (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D,E), raising the necessity to use caution when attempting to transform Drosophila sex by manipulating the fru locus.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D,E and citation to Yu et al., 2010.

claim: Optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL41-labeled neurons in fruM females induced lunges toward a fruF male target for the majority of testers.
source: Optogenetic activation of the Tk-GAL41-labeled neurons in fruM females induced lunges toward a fruF male target for the majority of testers (Figure 2A2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A2; see also Video 4 – Part 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2A2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A2.

claim: Optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL41-labeled neurons in fruM females increased orienting time during LED stimulations compared to during inter-stimulus intervals.
source: Although orienting time increased during LED stimulations compared to during ISIs (Figure 2A1, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A1), no overall change in the amount of wing extensions was observed compared to genetic controls (Figure 2A3).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2A1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A1.

claim: No overall change in the amount of wing extensions was observed in fruM females compared to genetic controls after optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL41-labeled neurons.
source: Although orienting time increased during LED stimulations compared to during ISIs (Figure 2A1, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A1), no overall change in the amount of wing extensions was observed compared to genetic controls (Figure 2A3).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2A3.

claim: Tk-GAL4FruM neurons are part of a fruM-dependent, but dsx-independent, neuronal circuit for male-type aggressive behavior.
source: This indicates that Tk-GAL4FruM neurons are part of a fruM-dependent, but dsx-independent, neuronal circuit for male-type aggressive behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that fruM females (which lack dsxM) can perform lunges when Tk-GAL4FruM neurons are activated.

claim: The motion sequence underlying the lunges observed in fruM females were indistinguishable from wild-type male lunges.
source: The motion sequence underlying the lunges observed in this genotype were indistinguishable from wild-type male lunges (Video 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by video evidence shown in Video 5.

claim: Forty-two percent of fruM females did not perform a single lunge after LED stimulation.
source: Forty-two percent (17/40) of fruM females did not perform a single lunge after LED stimulation (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative behavioral data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Over 96% of male testers lunged toward a male target after optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons.
source: In contrast, over 96% of male testers lunged toward a male target (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative behavioral data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The median of induced lunges observed in fruM females (2) was lower than observed for male testers (58).
source: The median of induced lunges observed in fruM females (2) was lower than observed for male testers (58).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of behavioral data.

claim: fruM females occasionally lunged toward a female target after optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL41-labeled neurons.
source: Second, fruM females occasionally lunged toward a female target (Video 4 – Part 2), in addition to a fruF male target.
evidence: This claim is supported by video evidence shown in Video 4 – Part 2.

claim: Male testers seldom lunge toward a female target after optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL41 neurons.
source: Even though lunges were induced even less frequently than toward fruF males (Figure 2A2, B2, C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A2, 2B2), it is still noteworthy because male testers seldom lunge toward a female target, even after optogenetic activation of the Tk-GAL41 neurons (Figure 1D2, Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1D2 and Figure 2C.

claim: Optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL41-labeled neurons in single-housed fruM females failed to induce a single lunge toward fruF male targets.
source: Interestingly, optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL41-labeled neurons in single-housed fruM females failed to induce a single lunge toward fruF male targets (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C2 F2).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C2 F2.

claim: Optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL41-labeled neurons in single-housed fruM females resulted in higher levels of orientation and wing extensions than exhibited by group-housed flies.
source: Instead, this manipulation resulted in higher levels of orientation and wing extensions than was exhibited by group-housed flies (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C1, C3).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C1, C3.

claim: The relatively high levels of courtship behavior seen in fruM females interferes with the aggression-promoting function of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons.
source: These data suggest that the relatively high levels of courtship behavior seen in fruM females interferes with the aggression-promoting function of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that single-housed fruM females (which show more courtship) do not lunge after optogenetic activation.

claim: Group-housed fruM females that did not lunge toward a target fly after optogenetic stimulation of Tk-GAL41-labeled neurons tended to show higher levels of wing extensions than testers who lunged.
source: Consistent with this idea, group-housed fruM females that did not lunge toward a target fly after optogenetic stimulation of Tk-GAL41-labeled neurons tended to show higher levels of wing extensions than testers who lunged (Figure 2—figure supplement 3E, F1).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3E, F1.

claim: Optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons did not induce headbutts in fruM females.
source: Lastly, optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons did not induce headbutts (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A3, B3), confirming that this genotype is using a male-type aggressive action exclusively (Vrontou et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A3, B3 and citation to Vrontou et al., 2006.

claim: The activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons induces lunges even in the absence of dsx-dependent aggression-promoting neurons.
source: The activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons induces lunges even in the absence of dsx-dependent aggression-promoting neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that fruM females (which lack male-type dsx-dependent neurons) can perform lunges when Tk-GAL4FruM neurons are activated.

claim: Tk-GAL4FruM neurons are part of a fruM-dependent execution mechanism for male aggressive behavior.
source: Tk-GAL4FruM neurons are therefore part of a fruM-dependent execution mechanism for male aggressive behavior (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral and anatomical data presented.

claim: A dsx-dependent mechanism may play a role in establishing a target sex-selective application of aggressive behavior.
source: However, the reduced intensity and compromised target sex selectivity of lunges shown by fruM females suggest that a dsx-dependent mechanism may play a role in establishing a target sex-selective application of aggressive behavior.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that fruM females show less selective aggression toward female targets compared to males.

claim: dsx can inhibit the execution of lunges specifically toward females.
source: This mechanism can inhibit the execution of lunges specifically toward females, which ensures that lunges are performed exclusively by males towards other males (Figure 2D), or can enhance aggression specifically toward male targets indirectly by inhibiting courtship toward them.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism by which dsx affects target sex selectivity.

claim: dsx can enhance aggression specifically toward male targets indirectly by inhibiting courtship toward them.
source: This mechanism can inhibit the execution of lunges specifically toward females, which ensures that lunges are performed exclusively by males towards other males (Figure 2D), or can enhance aggression specifically toward male targets indirectly by inhibiting courtship toward them.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism by which dsx affects target sex selectivity.

claim: dsx specifies the sexual dimorphism of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons.
source: As was discussed above, dsx specifies the sexual dimorphism of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons, such that the morphology of these neurons in fruM females is largely female-type, and not male-type (Figure 3A; see also Ishii et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 3A and citation to Ishii et al., 2020.

claim: The morphology of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in fruM females is largely female-type, and not male-type.
source: As was discussed above, dsx specifies the sexual dimorphism of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons, such that the morphology of these neurons in fruM females is largely female-type, and not male-type (Figure 3A; see also Ishii et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 3A and citation to Ishii et al., 2020.

claim: Optogenetic activation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in females robustly increased time orienting toward female target flies.
source: We confirmed that optogenetic activation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in females robustly increased time orienting (Figure 3C1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B1) and headbutts (Figure 3C2, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B2) toward female target flies, mostly during LED stimulation (see also Video 6 – Part 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3C1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B1.

claim: Optogenetic activation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in females robustly increased headbutts toward female target flies.
source: We confirmed that optogenetic activation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in females robustly increased time orienting (Figure 3C1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B1) and headbutts (Figure 3C2, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B2) toward female target flies, mostly during LED stimulation (see also Video 6 – Part 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3C2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B2.

claim: The behavioral phenotype of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neuron activation was consistently observed when the fru locus was either +/+, +/fru4-40 or fruF/fru4-40.
source: This behavioral phenotype was consistently observed when the fru locus was either +/+, +/fru4-40 or fruF/fru4-40, similar to the case in males (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Optogenetic activation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in females induced similar behaviors toward fruF male targets as toward female targets.
source: Interestingly, we observed similar behaviors toward the fruF male targets as well (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; see also Video 6 – Part 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons did not overlap with neurons labeled by the R71G01-LexA transgene.
source: However, we found that NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons did not overlap with neurons labeled by the R71G01-LexA transgene (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: Female 'pC1' neurons are anatomically and functionally heterogeneous.
source: This is consistent with recent findings that female 'pC1' neurons are anatomically and functionally heterogeneous (Deutsch et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Deutsch et al., 2020, Wang et al., 2020, and Wu et al., 2019.

claim: Optogenetic activation of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in fruM females did not induce lunges or headbutts.
source: Interestingly, we did not observe induction of either lunges or headbutts (Figure 3D2 and E2,3) when we optogenetically activated the NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in fruM females.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3D2 and E2,3.

claim: Female-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons can promote headbutts only if other mechanisms that rely on sexually dimorphic splicing of fru are present in the brain.
source: Thus, female-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons can promote headbutts only if other mechanisms that rely on sexually dimorphic splicing of fru are present in the brain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that female-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons do not promote headbutts in fruM females.

claim: Female-like NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons fail to establish functional connections with neurons that are part of the fruM-dependent execution mechanism for male-type aggression.
source: In addition, this result suggests that NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons with female-like morphology fail to establish functional connections with neurons that are part of the fruM-dependent execution mechanism for male-type aggression (which includes Tk-GAL4FruM neurons; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that female-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons do not promote aggression in fruM females.

claim: Female-like NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons cannot participate in generation of aggressive behavior without separate populations of neurons that are specified in the absence of fruM.
source: We therefore conclude that female-like NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons cannot participate in generation of aggressive behavior (e.g. headbutts) without separate populations of neurons that are specified in the absence of fruM.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that female-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons do not promote aggression in fruM females.

claim: The sexual dimorphism of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons does not determine the sexual dimorphism of aggressive actions.
source: This finding raises a possibility that the sexual dimorphism of NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons, which is largely specified by dsx, does not determine the sexual dimorphism of aggressive actions.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observation that female-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons do not promote aggression in fruM females.

claim: Male-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons cannot trigger lunges without a fruM-dependent mechanism.
source: As is shown in Ishii et al. (2020), male-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons cannot trigger lunges without a fruM-dependent mechanism, underscoring the dominant role of fru and fru-dependent neural circuits in specifying sexually dimorphic action patterns during aggressive interactions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ishii et al., 2020.

claim: fru has a dominant role in specifying sexually dimorphic action patterns during aggressive interactions.
source: As is shown in Ishii et al. (2020), male-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons cannot trigger lunges without a fruM-dependent mechanism, underscoring the dominant role of fru and fru-dependent neural circuits in specifying sexually dimorphic action patterns during aggressive interactions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that male-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons require fruM-dependent mechanisms to trigger lunges.

claim: fruM undergoes alternative splicing to create three transcript isoforms: fruMA, fruMB, and fruMC.
source: fruM undergoes another layer of alternative splicing to create three transcript isoforms, fruMA, fruMB, and fruMC, (Figure 4A), which encode different zinc finger domains (Usui-Aoki et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Usui-Aoki et al., 2000 and schematic shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The three fruM isoforms encode different zinc finger domains.
source: fruM undergoes another layer of alternative splicing to create three transcript isoforms, fruMA, fruMB, and fruMC, (Figure 4A), which encode different zinc finger domains (Usui-Aoki et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Usui-Aoki et al., 2000.

claim: The loss of each of three fruM isoforms affects male courtship behaviors in distinct manners.
source: The loss of each of three fruM isoforms is known to affect male courtship behaviors in distinct manners (Neville et al., 2014; von Philipsborn et al., 2014; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Neville et al., 2014 and von Philipsborn et al., 2014, as well as data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Loss of fruMA caused no reduction of lunges compared to the fru4-40 heterozygous genetic control.
source: Loss of fruMA caused no reduction of lunges compared to the fru4-40 heterozygous genetic control (Figure 4B2).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4B2.

claim: Loss of fruMB caused a dramatic reduction in male-type aggressive behaviors.
source: In contrast, we observed a dramatic reduction in male-type aggressive behaviors by the loss of fruMB or fruMC isoforms (Figure 4B2).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4B2.

claim: Loss of fruMC caused a dramatic reduction in male-type aggressive behaviors.
source: In contrast, we observed a dramatic reduction in male-type aggressive behaviors by the loss of fruMB or fruMC isoforms (Figure 4B2).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4B2.

claim: fruMC mutants showed decreased orientation time toward a male target.
source: While fruMC mutants showed decreased orientation time toward a male target, orienting times of fruMA and fruMB mutants were comparable to the fru4-40 heterozygous genetic control (Figure 4A1).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4A1 (note: the text says 4A1 but likely means 4B1).

claim: Orienting times of fruMA and fruMB mutants were comparable to the fru4-40 heterozygous genetic control.
source: While fruMC mutants showed decreased orientation time toward a male target, orienting times of fruMA and fruMB mutants were comparable to the fru4-40 heterozygous genetic control (Figure 4A1).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4A1 (note: the text says 4A1 but likely means 4B1).

claim: The reduction in lunges in fruMB mutants was qualitatively recapitulated when the fruF allele was used to create trans-heterozygotes.
source: This reduction in lunges in fruMB mutants was qualitatively recapitulated when the fruF allele was used to create trans-heterozygotes (Figure 4C), and when other mutations affecting FruB zinc finger domains (von Philipsborn et al., 2014) were tested in trans with fru4-40 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, as well as citation to von Philipsborn et al., 2014.

claim: No consistent reduction in overall activity levels was observed between fruMB mutants and genetic controls.
source: We observed no consistent reduction in overall activity levels between fruMB mutants and genetic controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), or in the total amount of sleep exhibited by these flies (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by activity data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: No consistent reduction in the total amount of sleep was observed between fruMB mutants and genetic controls.
source: We observed no consistent reduction in overall activity levels between fruMB mutants and genetic controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), or in the total amount of sleep exhibited by these flies (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by sleep data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Male-male courtship was differentially affected in the three fruM isoform mutants.
source: Male-male courtship was differentially affected in three mutants (Figure 4A3), reflecting varied degrees of courtship defects toward females (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B; Neville et al., 2014; von Philipsborn et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4A3 (note: likely means 4B3), Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B, and citations to Neville et al., 2014 and von Philipsborn et al., 2014.

claim: Each of the three fruM isoforms make different contributions to aggressive behaviors.
source: These data indicate that each of the three fruM isoforms make different contributions to aggressive behaviors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential effects of fruM isoform mutations on aggressive behavior.

claim: fruMA had a minimal impact on male aggressive behavior.
source: fruMA had a minimal impact on male aggressive behavior, whereas fruMB and fruMC were both necessary to maintain normal levels of male aggression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data showing no reduction in lunges in fruMA mutants.

claim: fruMB and fruMC were both necessary to maintain normal levels of male aggression.
source: fruMA had a minimal impact on male aggressive behavior, whereas fruMB and fruMC were both necessary to maintain normal levels of male aggression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data showing reduced lunges in fruMB and fruMC mutants.

claim: The decreased aggression of fruMB mutants was not necessarily due to reduced activity levels or opportunities to interact with the target fly.
source: Moreover, the decreased aggression of fruMB mutants was not necessarily due to reduced activity levels or opportunities to interact with the target fly.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that fruMB mutants show normal activity levels and orienting time.

claim: In fruMC mutants, only 1.9 ± 1.1 faintly labeled neurons were found in the brain area where Tk-GAL4FruM neurons are expected to appear.
source: In fruMC mutants, we found only 1.9 ± 1.1 (mean ± S.D., n = 8; Figure 5D,E) faintly labeled neurons in the brain area where Tk-GAL4FruM neurons are expected to appear, significantly fewer than the number of cells found in genetic controls (5.6 ± 0.5, mean ± S.D., n = 8; Figure 5A,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative anatomical data shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: The number of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in fruMC mutants was significantly fewer than in genetic controls.
source: In fruMC mutants, we found only 1.9 ± 1.1 (mean ± S.D., n = 8; Figure 5D,E) faintly labeled neurons in the brain area where Tk-GAL4FruM neurons are expected to appear, significantly fewer than the number of cells found in genetic controls (5.6 ± 0.5, mean ± S.D., n = 8; Figure 5A,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative anatomical data shown in Figure 5A,E.

claim: fruMA and fruMB mutants did not affect the number of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons.
source: In contrast, fruMA and fruMB mutants did not affect the number of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative anatomical data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Tk-GAL4FruM neurons from fruMA or fruMB mutants are indistinguishable from each other or from fru4-40 heterozygous control males.
source: Tk-GAL4FruM neurons from fruMA (Figure 5G) or fruMB (Figure 5H) mutants are indistinguishable from each other or from fru4-40 heterozygous control males (Figure 5F; see also Video 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by registered and averaged imaging data shown in Figure 5F-H and Video 7.

claim: No significant differences in volumes of three prominent neurites of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons were detected among fru4-40 heterozygous controls, fruMA mutants, and fruMB mutants.
source: We measured the volumes of three prominent neurites that emanate from the lateral junction (Yu et al., 2010) of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons (Figure 5F2–H2; see also Figure 1L1, M1), and detected no significant differences among fru4-40 heterozygous controls, fruMA mutants, and fruMB mutants (Figure 5I–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative volume measurements shown in Figure 5I–K and citation to Yu et al., 2010.

claim: Heterozygosity of all isoform-specific mutations did not change the cell body number or gross morphology of the Tk-GAL4FruM neurons.
source: Heterozygosity of all isoform-specific mutations did not change the cell body number or gross morphology of the Tk-GAL4FruM neurons (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D), either.
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: fruMA, fruMB and fruMC have distinct effects on male aggression and specification of the Tk-GAL4FruM neurons.
source: Taken together, we found that fruMA, fruMB and fruMC have distinct effects on male aggression and specification of the Tk-GAL4FruM neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral and anatomical data on fruM isoform mutants.

claim: fruMA appeared largely dispensable for both male aggression and specification of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons.
source: fruMA appeared largely dispensable for both, whereas fruMC was necessary for both.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral and anatomical data on fruMA mutants.

claim: fruMC was necessary for both male aggression and specification of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons.
source: fruMA appeared largely dispensable for both, whereas fruMC was necessary for both.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral and anatomical data on fruMC mutants.

claim: fruMB was necessary for normal levels of male-male aggression, but was not required for specification of the Tk-GAL4FruM neurons.
source: Interestingly, fruMB was necessary for normal levels of male-male aggression, but was not required for specification of the Tk-GAL4FruM neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral and anatomical data on fruMB mutants.

claim: The overall calcium response dynamics and magnitudes of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in fruMB mutants were comparable to those seen in the fru4-40 heterozygous controls.
source: The overall calcium response dynamics and magnitudes of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in fruMB mutants were comparable to those seen in the fru4-40 heterozygous controls (Figure 6C,D), suggesting that Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in fruMB mutants are capable of physiologically responding to depolarizing stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in fruMB mutants are capable of physiologically responding to depolarizing stimuli.
source: The overall calcium response dynamics and magnitudes of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in fruMB mutants were comparable to those seen in the fru4-40 heterozygous controls (Figure 6C,D), suggesting that Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in fruMB mutants are capable of physiologically responding to depolarizing stimuli.
evidence: This is an inference based on the calcium imaging data showing normal responses in fruMB mutants.

claim: Optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL41-labeled neurons in fruMB mutants elicited robust levels of male aggression across several LED intensities.
source: Optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL41-labeled neurons in fruMB mutants elicited robust levels of male aggression across several LED intensities, as seen in genetic controls (Figure 6E–G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6E–G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in fruMB mutants, once activated, can induce male aggression as efficiently as in the fru wild-type males.
source: This result suggests that Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in fruMB mutants, once activated, can induce male aggression as efficiently as in the fru wild-type males, and argues against the hypothesis that the mutation of fruMB proteins causes defective development of downstream neurons or reduced efficiency of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons to excite downstream neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in fruMB mutants induces normal levels of aggression.

claim: fruMB mutation reduces aggression-promoting input to Tk-GAL4FruM neurons from upstream circuits.
source: Instead, these results favor the alternative hypothesis that fruMB mutation reduces aggression-promoting input to Tk-GAL4FruM neurons from upstream circuits.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the observation that fruMB mutants show reduced spontaneous aggression but normal aggression when Tk-GAL4FruM neurons are optogenetically activated.

claim: Three isoforms of fruM assume distinct roles in the specification and function of sexually dimorphic neurons that control male-type aggressive behaviors.
source: Overall, our results show that three isoforms of fruM assume distinct roles in the specification and function of sexually dimorphic neurons that control male-type aggressive behaviors (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral, anatomical, and functional data on fruM isoform mutants.

claim: fruMC is necessary for the specification of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons.
source: Namely, fruMC is necessary for the specification of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons, whereas fruMB is necessary for a normal level of spontaneous aggression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the anatomical data showing reduced Tk-GAL4FruM neuron numbers in fruMC mutants.

claim: fruMB is necessary for a normal level of spontaneous aggression.
source: Namely, fruMC is necessary for the specification of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons, whereas fruMB is necessary for a normal level of spontaneous aggression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data showing reduced spontaneous aggression in fruMB mutants.

claim: Tk-GAL4FruM neurons and downstream populations form a neural circuit that is sufficient for the execution of male-type aggressive behavior.
source: We found that the optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in fruM female tester flies induced male-type aggressive behavior. This result indicates that at least Tk-GAL4FruM neurons and downstream populations form a neural circuit that is sufficient for the execution of male-type aggressive behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that optogenetic activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons in fruM females induces lunges.

claim: Neurons specified by fru form the execution mechanism for male-type aggressive action.
source: These observations favor a hypothesis that neurons specified by fru, which include Tk-GAL4FruM neurons, form the execution mechanism for male-type aggressive action, and NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons serve as modulatory neurons that act on this fru-dependent execution mechanism.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that Tk-GAL4FruM neurons (specified by fru) can induce lunges in fruM females.

claim: NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons serve as modulatory neurons that act on the fru-dependent execution mechanism.
source: These observations favor a hypothesis that neurons specified by fru, which include Tk-GAL4FruM neurons, form the execution mechanism for male-type aggressive action, and NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons serve as modulatory neurons that act on this fru-dependent execution mechanism.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons do not induce aggression in fruM females.

claim: Sex-specific splicing of fru defines what type of aggressive behavior an animal performs.
source: Sex-specific splicing of fru defines what type of aggressive behavior an animal performs, likely by specifying a mutually exclusive neural circuit that generates either male-type or female-type aggressive actions.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that fruM females perform male-type aggression.

claim: dsx is important for suppressing inappropriate aggressive behavior toward a female target.
source: In fact, fruM females lunge against females as well as fruF males, suggesting that dsx is important for suppressing inappropriate aggressive behavior toward a female target.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that fruM females (which lack dsxM) lunge toward female targets.

claim: dsx-expressing neurons respond to sex-specific sensory cues, such as olfactory, gustatory, and auditory stimuli.
source: Intriguingly, however, dsx-expressing neurons respond to sex-specific sensory cues, such as olfactory, gustatory, and auditory stimuli (Deutsch et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Deutsch et al., 2019, Zhou et al., 2014, and Zhou et al., 2015.

claim: Thermogenetic activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons induces lunges toward a male target that lacks cuticular hydrocarbons.
source: Since thermogenetic activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons induces lunges toward a male target that lacks cuticular hydrocarbons (Asahina et al., 2014), one possible scenario is that a dsx-dependent circuit is responsible for detection or transmission of female-specific, aggression-suppressing cues that have yet to be identified.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Asahina et al., 2014.

claim: A dsx-dependent circuit may be responsible for detection or transmission of female-specific, aggression-suppressing cues.
source: Since thermogenetic activation of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons induces lunges toward a male target that lacks cuticular hydrocarbons (Asahina et al., 2014), one possible scenario is that a dsx-dependent circuit is responsible for detection or transmission of female-specific, aggression-suppressing cues that have yet to be identified.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the role of dsx in target sex selectivity.

claim: dsx in males may allow execution of male-type aggressive behavior specifically toward male targets indirectly by inhibiting courtship behavior toward males.
source: Alternatively, dsx in males may allow execution of male-type aggressive behavior specifically toward male targets indirectly by inhibiting courtship behavior toward males.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the role of dsx in target sex selectivity.

claim: Courtship behavior can interfere with aggressive behavior, possibly through feedforward inhibitory circuits.
source: fruM females that showed high levels of courtship behavior generally showed low levels of male-type aggression. This observation suggests that courtship behavior can interfere with aggressive behavior, possibly through feedforward inhibitory circuits (Clowney et al., 2015; Kallman et al., 2015; Koganezawa et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that fruM females with high courtship show low aggression, supported by citations to Clowney et al., 2015, Kallman et al., 2015, and Koganezawa et al., 2016.

claim: Information about target sex can be supplied downstream of Tk-GAL4FruM neuronal activities and modify its behavioral influence.
source: The contribution of dsx on the target sex-selective execution of aggressive behavior also implies that information about target sex can be supplied downstream of Tk-GAL4FruM neuronal activities and modify its behavioral influence.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that dsx affects target sex selectivity of aggression.

claim: dsx-specified neurons may serve as a 'block' against neuronal activity generated by Tk-GAL4FruM neurons and other unidentified constituents of the lunge execution mechanism.
source: It is possible that dsx-specified neurons serve as a 'block' against neuronal activity generated by Tk-GAL4FruM neurons and other unidentified constituents of the lunge execution mechanism.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism by which dsx affects target sex selectivity.

claim: NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in females promote female-type aggression.
source: Consistent with a previous observation (Koganezawa et al., 2016), we observed that NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons in females promote female-type aggression.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data and citation to Koganezawa et al., 2016.

claim: NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons belong to a cluster of dsx-expressing 'pC1' neurons.
source: This population belongs to a cluster of dsx-expressing 'pC1' neurons, which is known to promote a variety of female social behaviors including aggression (Deutsch et al., 2020; Palavicino-Maggio et al., 2019; Robie et al., 2017), receptivity (Deutsch et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2014) or even courtship-like behaviors (Rezával et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Deutsch et al., 2020, Palavicino-Maggio et al., 2019, Robie et al., 2017, Zhou et al., 2014, Rezával et al., 2016, and Wu et al., 2019.

claim: 'pC1' neurons promote a variety of female social behaviors including aggression, receptivity, and courtship-like behaviors.
source: This population belongs to a cluster of dsx-expressing 'pC1' neurons, which is known to promote a variety of female social behaviors including aggression (Deutsch et al., 2020; Palavicino-Maggio et al., 2019; Robie et al., 2017), receptivity (Deutsch et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2014) or even courtship-like behaviors (Rezával et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Deutsch et al., 2020, Palavicino-Maggio et al., 2019, Robie et al., 2017, Zhou et al., 2014, Rezával et al., 2016, and Wu et al., 2019.

claim: Female-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons are unlikely to be a part of the execution mechanism that generates female-type aggressive actions.
source: In spite of the importance of 'pC1' neurons collectively on female social behaviors, female-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons are unlikely to be a part of the execution mechanism that generates female-type aggressive actions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that female-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons do not promote aggression in fruM females.

claim: There are uncharacterized sexually dimorphic neurons that are necessary for females to execute headbutts and other female-specific aggressive actions.
source: Our results suggest that there are uncharacterized sexually dimorphic neurons that are necessary for females to execute headbutts and other female-specific aggressive actions, likely downstream of female-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observation that female-type NP2631 ∩ dsxFLP neurons do not promote aggression in fruM females.

claim: fruMC is important for the specification of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons.
source: Our result is in line with the previously reported importance of the fruMC isoform in the development of male-specific branching patterns in several fruM-expressing neurons (Billeter et al., 2006; Ito et al., 2016; von Philipsborn et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the anatomical data and supported by citations to Billeter et al., 2006, Ito et al., 2016, and von Philipsborn et al., 2014.

claim: fruMC is important for the development of male-specific branching patterns in several fruM-expressing neurons.
source: Our result is in line with the previously reported importance of the fruMC isoform in the development of male-specific branching patterns in several fruM-expressing neurons (Billeter et al., 2006; Ito et al., 2016; von Philipsborn et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Billeter et al., 2006, Ito et al., 2016, and von Philipsborn et al., 2014.

claim: Activities of 'P1' neurons are necessary for normal levels of courtship behavior.
source: Among them, activities of 'P1' neurons (von Philipsborn et al., 2014) and mAL/aDT2 neurons (Ito et al., 2016; von Philipsborn et al., 2014) are necessary for normal levels of courtship behavior (Kallman et al., 2015; von Philipsborn et al., 2011), reflecting the severe courtship defects of fruMC mutant males (Neville et al., 2014; von Philipsborn et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to von Philipsborn et al., 2014, Kallman et al., 2015, and von Philipsborn et al., 2011.

claim: Activities of mAL/aDT2 neurons are necessary for normal levels of courtship behavior.
source: Among them, activities of 'P1' neurons (von Philipsborn et al., 2014) and mAL/aDT2 neurons (Ito et al., 2016; von Philipsborn et al., 2014) are necessary for normal levels of courtship behavior (Kallman et al., 2015; von Philipsborn et al., 2011), reflecting the severe courtship defects of fruMC mutant males (Neville et al., 2014; von Philipsborn et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ito et al., 2016, von Philipsborn et al., 2014, Kallman et al., 2015, and von Philipsborn et al., 2011.

claim: fruMC mutant males show severe courtship defects.
source: Among them, activities of 'P1' neurons (von Philipsborn et al., 2014) and mAL/aDT2 neurons (Ito et al., 2016; von Philipsborn et al., 2014) are necessary for normal levels of courtship behavior (Kallman et al., 2015; von Philipsborn et al., 2011), reflecting the severe courtship defects of fruMC mutant males (Neville et al., 2014; von Philipsborn et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Neville et al., 2014 and von Philipsborn et al., 2014.

claim: fruMC is necessary for both male aggression and specification of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons at behavioral and circuitry levels.
source: Our observation that fruMC is necessary for both male aggression and specification of Tk-GAL4FruM neurons reveals its importance for male-type aggressive behavior as well, at behavioral and circuitry levels.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral and anatomical data on fruMC mutants.

claim: fruMC can be regarded as exerting 'organizational' functions.
source: Using an analogy from the function of steroid hormones in mammals (McCarthy, 2008), fruMC can be regarded as exerting 'organizational' functions, while fruMB may exert 'activation' functions, in the sense that fruMB is dispensable for the specification of a lunge execution mechanism, yet is necessary for induction of spontaneous aggressive behaviors.
evidence: This is an analogy drawn from mammalian steroid hormone function, supported by citation to McCarthy, 2008.

claim: fruMB may exert 'activation' functions.
source: Using an analogy from the function of steroid hormones in mammals (McCarthy, 2008), fruMC can be regarded as exerting 'organizational' functions, while fruMB may exert 'activation' functions, in the sense that fruMB is dispensable for the specification of a lunge execution mechanism, yet is necessary for induction of spontaneous aggressive behaviors.
evidence: This is an analogy drawn from mammalian steroid hormone function, supported by citation to McCarthy, 2008.

claim: The segregation of roles within fru isoforms may increase the gene's flexibility.
source: The segregation of roles within fru isoforms may increase the gene's flexibility: for instance, change in the circuit connectivity underlying perception of male-specific cues can be independently altered if different isoforms have different roles in the aggression circuit.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the evolutionary implications of fru isoform diversity.

claim: There are at least 3 different estrogen receptor genes in mice.
source: In mice, there are at least 3 different estrogen receptor genes (Wu et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wu et al., 2009.

claim: A similar type of division of labor may exist among the estrogen receptor genes in mice.
source: Although the specific function of each receptor on neural circuits that control sexual behaviors remains largely uncharacterized, it is tempting to speculate that a similar type of division of labor may exist among the estrogen receptor genes.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the function of estrogen receptor genes in mice.

claim: Each sex-determining gene controls specific aspects of sexually dimorphic traits, including behaviors.
source: Our results suggest that one of the reasons behind this apparent genetic cooperativity may be that each gene controls specific aspects of sexually dimorphic traits, including behaviors (Pereira et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential roles of dsx and fru, supported by citations to Pereira et al., 2019 and Xu et al., 2012.

claim: Separate genetic mechanisms for establishing sexually dimorphic actions and target sex-dependent action bias may be evolutionarily adaptive.
source: We further speculate that separate genetic mechanisms for establishing sexually dimorphic actions and target sex-dependent action bias may be evolutionarily adaptive.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the evolutionary implications of separate genetic mechanisms.

claim: dsx plays an important role in specifying the male courtship execution circuit.
source: In Ishii et al. (2020), we showed that dsx plays an important role in specifying the male courtship execution circuit.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ishii et al., 2020.

claim: The dsx gene produces functional proteins in both sexes.
source: The dsx gene produces functional proteins in both sexes, and mediates specification of not only male-type circuits for courtship but also female-type circuits that make females receptive to such motor programs (Deutsch et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Deutsch et al., 2019 and Zhou et al., 2014.

claim: dsx mediates specification of male-type circuits for courtship and female-type circuits that make females receptive to such motor programs.
source: The dsx gene produces functional proteins in both sexes, and mediates specification of not only male-type circuits for courtship but also female-type circuits that make females receptive to such motor programs (Deutsch et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Deutsch et al., 2019 and Zhou et al., 2014.

claim: The dual function of dsx in males and females may ensure that the species-specificity of courtship rituals are preserved between both sexes even during speciation.
source: This dual function of dsx in males and females may ensure that the species-specificity of courtship rituals are preserved between both sexes even during speciation, which must accompany co-evolution of both a male's courtship behavior and a female's choice process through sexual selection (Majerus, 1986).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the evolutionary implications of dsx function, supported by citation to Majerus, 1986.

claim: dsx-expressing neurons show high selectivity to courtship pulse song with behaviorally relevant inter-pulse interval frequencies both in males and females.
source: Interestingly, dsx-expressing neurons show high selectivity to courtship pulse song with behaviorally relevant inter-pulse interval frequencies both in males and females (Deutsch et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Deutsch et al., 2019 and Zhou et al., 2015.

claim: Aggressive behavior is executed by sexually dimorphic motor programs often between two members of the same sex, most predominantly among males.
source: In contrast, aggressive behavior is executed by sexually dimorphic motor programs often between two members of the same sex, most predominantly among males (Chen et al., 2002; Nilsen et al., 2004; Smith and Price, 1973).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2002, Nilsen et al., 2004, and Smith and Price, 1973.

claim: Sexually dimorphic traits that bring advantage specifically during inter-male competition can be fixed through evolution even if it is not directly under sexual selection.
source: Consequently, aggressive actions can be under a different selection pressure from courtship behavior. Ample examples of male-specific weaponry organs across a variety of species support the hypothesis that sexually dimorphic traits that bring advantage specifically during inter-male competition can be fixed through evolution even if it is not directly under sexual selection (Rico-Guevara and Hurme, 2018).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation to Rico-Guevara and Hurme, 2018.

claim: Some closely related Hawaiian Drosophila species evolved species-specific aggressive rituals even though action patterns of courtship behavior as well as morphology of antennae remain relatively similar.
source: Indeed, some closely related Hawaiian Drosophila species evolved species-specific aggressive rituals even though action patterns of courtship behavior as well as morphology of antennae, an organ necessary for successful courtship, remain relatively similar (Kaneshiro and Boake, 1987; Price and Boake, 1995; Spieth, 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kaneshiro and Boake, 1987, Price and Boake, 1995, and Spieth, 1981.

claim: Animals must be equipped with a genetic mechanism that controls motor programs for aggressive behavior at least partially separately from the motor programs for courtship behavior.
source: This example suggests that animals must be equipped with a genetic mechanism that controls motor programs for aggressive behavior at least partially separately from the motor programs for courtship behavior.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that aggressive rituals can evolve independently of courtship behavior.

claim: fru is well situated to be a genetic agent for male-specific modification of aggressive behavior.
source: fru is well situated to be a genetic agent for such a male-specific modification of aggressive behavior (Davis et al., 2000), because it seems dispensable for specifying a neural circuit that generates at least certain aspects of courtship action patterns (see Ishii et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that fru is important for aggression but not for certain aspects of courtship, supported by citations to Davis et al., 2000 and Ishii et al., 2020.

claim: dsx can ensure that males do not act aggressively toward a conspecific female.
source: At the same time, dsx can ensure that males do not act aggressively toward a conspecific female.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that dsx affects target sex selectivity of aggression.

claim: Female-type somatic characteristics, including sex-specific chemical cues, are specified by dsx.
source: Female-type somatic characteristics, including sex-specific chemical cues (Shirangi et al., 2009), are specified by dsx.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Shirangi et al., 2009.
